import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The Para API offers a few options for authentication. Para API clients can call the API authenticated either as *users* or *apps*:

| Principal | Method | Credentials | Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| App | Signed request (AWS v4) | Access key and secret key | **Full API access** |
| App | App JWT | Signed with app's secret key | **Full API access** |
| User | User JWT, also called a personal access token (PAT) | Signed with user's secret + app secret | **Restricted API access** (see [resource permissions](/docs/concepts/resource-permissions/)) |

Use signed requests for server-side apps. A super JWT is an option for clients that cannot sign requests, but it requires
the app secret key. A user JWT identifies an individual user and never grants app-level access.
This auth method is suitable for insecure client-side code or mobile apps.

<Aside type="note" title="Initial setup is automatic">

When Para starts for the first time, it creates the root app (`app:para` by default) and writes the generated root
credentials to `para-application.conf`. If you set `para.root_secret_override`, Para uses that secret instead and does
not generate one. The generated credentials look like this:

```ini title="para-application.conf"
para.root_access_key = "app:para"
para.root_secret_key = "secret"
```

You do not need to call `GET /v1/_setup` for first-time setup. To create additional apps, call
`GET /v1/_setup/{app_name}` with a request signed by the root app, or use the Para CLI. See
[Apps](/docs/concepts/apps/).

</Aside>

### Signed requests

Para uses the **AWS Signature Version 4** algorithm to sign API requests. All Para client libraries use this method for
API authentication.

A signed request includes the access key and is signed with the secret key. The secret key is never sent in the request.
A request that is signed correctly has full access to the app API.

We recommend that you use one of our API client libraries to handle signing. See
[Para client libraries](/docs/getting-started/quickstart/#para-client-libraries).

<Aside type="note">

When a resource has public permissions you can access it without setting the `Authorization` header.
Simply specify your access key as a parameter:

```
GET /v1/public/resource?accessKey=app:myapp
```

</Aside>

### Full access with app JWTs ("super" tokens)

A super JWT is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that authenticates an app, not a user. It has no user subject and gives full access
to the app API. Para accepts it as a Bearer token.

The token must:

- use the `HS256` algorithm
- contain the `appid` claim
- be signed with the app secret key

Only trusted clients should create super tokens. **Do not put the app secret key in browser or mobile code.** Generate
the token on a server, or use a signed request instead.

To create a super token in JavaScript, use a JWT library such as
[jsrsasign](https://github.com/kjur/jsrsasign):

```js
function getJWT(appid, secret) {
	var now = Math.round(new Date().getTime() / 1000);
	var sClaim = JSON.stringify({
		exp: now + (7 * 24 * 60 * 60), // expires at
		iat: now, // issued at
		nbf: now, // not valid before
		appid: appid // app id must be present
	});
	var sHeader = JSON.stringify({'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'});
	return KJUR.jws.JWS.sign(null, sHeader, sClaim, secret);
}
```

The example uses a seven-day expiry. Change it to match your security requirements.

Attach the token to every request:

```js
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOi0._MKAH6SGiKSoqgwmqUaxuMyE
```

When you call the Para API from JavaScript in the browser, make sure you run a web server and not `file:///`, or your
browser might not allow CORS requests. Also check that CORS is enabled in Para with `para.cors_enabled = true`.

### Changing the app's secret key

Call `POST /v1/_newkeys` with a request signed by the current keys to generate a new secret key. The access key does not
change, and Para shows the new secret key only once.


### Example: Calling the API from Postman or Insomnia

You can access the protected API from a REST client like Postman or Insomnia, since those two support the AWS Signature v4 algorithm, used in Para.
Open up Postman and in the "Authorization" tab choose "AWS Signature":

<div class="text-center">
<img class="img-responsive" alt="Postman Authorization tab with the AWS Signature type selected" width="405" height="280" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="max-width:100%;height:auto" src="data:image/png;base64," />
</div>

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Access Key** | Your Para access key, e.g. `app:myapp`. |
| **Secret Key** | Your Para secret key. |
| **Region** | Always `us-east-1`. |
| **Service Name** | Always `para`. |

**Make sure you don't have extra headers** in your requests because Postman is known to calculate invalid signatures for such requests.

## User access

Users do not receive app keys. A user signs in through an identity provider, and Para returns a user JWT. This token is
also called a personal access token (PAT). It grants restricted access to the user's own objects and to resources allowed
by the app's [resource permissions](/docs/concepts/resource-permissions/).

<Aside type="caution">

A user JWT cannot access the root app. User sign-in is only available for apps other than the root app.

</Aside>

### Get a user JWT

Call `POST /jwt_auth` with the app ID, the provider, and the provider token:

```http
POST /jwt_auth
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "appid": "app:myapp",
  "provider": "password",
  "token": "user@example.com::password123"
}
```

The response contains the JWT and the user object:

```json
{
  "jwt": {
    "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...",
    "expires": 1450738414000,
    "refresh": 1450137214490
  },
  "user": {
    "id": "587408205806571520"
  }
}
```

Send the access token in the `Authorization` header:

```http
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
```

The token expires after 24 hours by default. You can change this with `para.jwt_expires_after`. Para client libraries
refresh the token automatically before it expires.

### Example: User auth with the Java client

The Para client handles sign-in, token storage, and token refresh:

```java
User user = paraClient.signIn("facebook", "facebook_access_token");
```

Supported providers are `facebook`, `google`, `twitter`, `github`, `linkedin`, `microsoft`, `slack`, `amazon`,
`password`, `oauth2`, `oauth2second`, `oauth2third`, `ldap`, and `passwordless`.

After `paraClient.signIn()` succeeds, the client caches the token and **all subsequent requests** to the API include it
until `paraClient.signOut()` is called.

To get or set access tokens use:

```java
paraClient.getAccessToken();
paraClient.setAccessToken(String token);
```

To sign out and clear the token use:

```java
paraClient.signOut();
```

To invalidate all tokens for the signed-in user use:

```java
paraClient.revokeAllTokens();
```

<details>
<summary>Provider configuration example</summary>

For the browser sign-in flow, add the provider credentials to your `para-application.conf` configuration file. The
REST `POST /jwt_auth` call uses a provider token, so it does not use these OAuth client credentials.

```ini title="para-application.conf"
# facebook
para.fb_app_id = "..."
para.fb_secret = "..."
# google
para.gp_app_id = "..."
para.gp_secret = "..."
# linkedin
para.in_app_id = "..."
para.in_secret = "..."
# twitter
para.tw_app_id = "..."
para.tw_secret = "..."
# github
para.gh_app_id = "..."
para.gh_secret = "..."
# microsoft
para.ms_app_id = "..."
para.ms_secret = "..."
# slack
para.sl_app_id = "..."
para.sl_secret = "..."
# amazon
para.az_app_id = "..."
para.az_secret = "..."
# generic oauth2
para.oa2_app_id = "..."
para.oa2_secret = "..."
# second generic oauth2
para.oa2second_app_id = "..."
para.oa2second_secret = "..."
# third generic oauth2
para.oa2third_app_id = "..."
para.oa2third_secret = "..."
```

See the [identity provider pages](/docs/security/id-providers/facebook/) for provider-specific setup.

</details>
